newsitem.title: USA: Mass. Senate budget to abolish county government.
newsitem.headline: Mass. Senate budget to abolish county government.

text.p: County government will be effectively abolished in the Massachusetts Senate budget, the chairman of the powerful Ways and Means committee said Tuesday.

Ways and Means Chairman Stanley Rosenberg (D-Amherst) said the state must spend $25.6 million next year in order to absorb the remaining functions of counties, including the registries of deeds, county jails, and county courthouses.

Sheriffs and the registers of deeds will continue as elected officials, county vocational schools will be unchanged, and district attorneys - state employees since 1978 - will retain their districts, under Rosenberg's plan.
"We're not abolishing counties, we're abolishing county government," said Sen. Richard Moore (D-Uxbridge), vice-chairman of the Counties Committee.
Moore explained that the registries and sherrifs had both filed separate legislation early this year, requesting state takeover.

Rosenberg was quick to note the takeover of registries and jails was already planned in last year's budget, and is scheduled to take effect July 1, 1997. He presented the provisions in the fiscal year 1998 budget as a means of finishing a job already started.
"If you remove those two (agencies), you're left with a shell of a government," he said.
The push for abolishing counties, in the works for several years, gathered steam in December 1996, when Middlesex County defaulted on a $4.5 million loan for Middlesex Hospital.
Several of the county's creditors filed suit, drawing attention to the total accumulated $45 million debt of Massachusetts' 14 counties.

Under the Ways and Means proposal, cities and towns in debt-ridden counties would amortize and repay the deficit. The committee will hold another briefing Wednesday, and release the entire budget on Thursday. ((--Boston bureau, 617-367-4106))
